extract:
André De Shields is an American actor, singer, director, and choreographer whose recorded presence on Spotify comes almost entirely from Broadway cast albums. Born on January 12, 1946, in Baltimore, Maryland, he has worked on stage for more than five decades. He is best known to contemporary listeners as Hermes, the silver-suited narrator of Anaïs Mitchell's Hadestown. The tracks listed under his name, including Road to Hell, its reprise, Wait for Me, and the spoken intros and outros, come from that show's 2019 Original Broadway Cast Recording.

De Shields was one of eleven children and grew up in segregated Baltimore. He later studied at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. His early theatrical education came partly through Chicago's countercultural scene, where he appeared in a production of Hair at the end of the 1960s. The exuberant, rock-inflected style of that era, along with the Black vaudeville and jazz traditions he absorbed, shaped a performing persona built on elegance, showmanship, and an unmistakably rich speaking voice.

His Broadway breakthrough came in 1975, when he created the title role in The Wiz, Charlie Smalls's soul-and-funk reimagining of The Wizard of Oz. In 1978 he joined the original cast of Ain't Misbehavin', the Fats Waller revue conceived by Richard Maltby Jr. The show became a landmark of the decade, and De Shields won an Emmy Award for the televised version broadcast on NBC in 1982. He conceived and starred in Harlem Nocturne in the 1980s. He earned Tony nominations for Play On!, a Duke Ellington musical set in Harlem, and for The Full Monty in 2000, where his character Noah "Horse" T. Simmons stopped the show with the number "Big Black Man." Across these roles he became a link between the jazz-age songbook and modern musical theater.

Hadestown gave De Shields his most widely heard recordings. Directed by Rachel Chavkin, with orchestrations by Michael Chorney and Todd Sickafoose, the folk-and-New-Orleans-jazz retelling of the Orpheus and Eurydice myth casts Hermes as a sly master of ceremonies. On the cast album he opens the show with Road to Hell, sets up scenes in spoken intros such as When the Chips are Down, and delivers the gentle, fatherly guidance of Wait for Me. He shared the stage with Reeve Carney, Eva Noblezada, Amber Gray, and Patrick Page. The cast recording won the Grammy Award for Best Musical Theater Album.

The role finally brought him a Tony Award in 2019, for Best Featured Actor in a Musical. His acceptance speech became widely quoted for its "three cardinal rules on sustaining longevity in this business":

1. Surround yourself with people whose eyes light up when they see you coming.
2. Slowly is the fastest way to get to where you want to be.
3. The top of one mountain is the bottom of the next, so keep climbing.

The speech, together with his age and decades of persistence, turned the moment into one of the ceremony's most celebrated.

De Shields's legacy spans roughly half a century of Black musical theater, from The Wiz and Ain't Misbehavin' to Hadestown. He has continued to work as a performer, teacher, and speaker, and he is regarded as an elder statesman of Broadway whose career demonstrates the endurance he described in that speech.
title: André De Shields
